NCP: Verifier-Guided Optimization of Weight-Space Control Policies

Ekrem Aksoy
November 5, 2026
Abstract

We present the Neural Control Plane (NCP), a closed-loop system that observes language-model execution, synthesizes candidate weight-space intervention rules, evaluates them, and maintains a versioned table of admitted policies. NCP separates a pretrained model’s inference data plane from the control policy that selects temporary parameter interventions. W-ISA supplies transactional execution and parameter restoration; NCP supplies telemetry, candidate synthesis, admission criteria, priorities, and rule lifetime management. The optimization state consists of active rules and an archive of evaluated candidates, while base-model parameters are restored after each request. In a local SmolLM-135M-Instruct experiment, NCP generated three candidates from development telemetry and evaluated them on separate task examples and a 4,095-target WikiText-2 slice. One projection reduced validation token repetition from 0.4133 to 0.2191, with a perplexity change of -0.0574%. All candidates produced zero newly correct exact answers, so the configured admission gate archived all three and retained the original active policy. Fresh-process repetition and saved-table resumption reproduced the measured outcomes. NCP provides an executable framework for studying recursive self-improvement at the control-policy level through explicit synthesis, verification, and state transitions.

Keywords: neural control plane; recursive self-improvement; inference-time optimization; weight-space interventions; model editing; transactional execution.

1 Introduction

Inference-time adaptation can be expressed through changes to prompts, intermediate activations, auxiliary memory, or model parameters. Each choice creates a different optimization state and execution lifecycle. NCP studies the policy that decides which weight-space intervention to apply to an incoming request.

We explicitly credit Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab’s Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights [11] as a conceptual foundation. Their November 2, 2026 article presents reasoning-driven weight inspection and editing, describes a tool-assisted loop-reduction experiment on Qwen3.5-0.8B, and identifies recursive self-improvement as a research direction. NCP develops a verifier-guided control-policy architecture around this weight-space programming perspective, using W-ISA for scoped execution.

The system observes task outcomes and output-token telemetry, extracts an activation direction associated with development failures, and constructs explicit match-action candidates. A verifier compares the current policy with the policy that would result from admitting each candidate. Accepted rules become part of the active flow table; evaluation records preserve the outcomes of every trial.

Our architectural starting point is the separation of control and data planes used in software-defined networking. OpenFlow provides a flow-table interface through which a controller manages packet-processing behavior [1]. NCP adopts this separation as a software design: the language model performs tensor computation, the W-ISA runtime executes parameter interventions, and the controller selects and evaluates rules.

The recursive self-improvement (RSI) research objective is improvement of this control policy across successive feedback cycles. An admitted rule changes the behavior observed in later requests, which changes subsequent telemetry and candidate generation. The implemented loop uses a deterministic synthesizer and an explicit verifier, making each proposed policy transition inspectable.

The central question is:

Can a language-model control policy be improved through repeated generation, temporary execution, and verification of activation-conditioned weight-space rules while preserving a stable base parameter state?

The present contribution is an executable architecture for this question: a versioned neural flow table, deterministic candidate generation, a routed-task and forced-action admission gate, and a reproducible local evaluation protocol.

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Weight-space programming

Takehi et al. [11] study general-purpose LLMs reading and writing weights under natural-language objectives, including experiments with controlled forward-pass budgets. Their discussion of model correction and recursive self-improvement motivates the NCP research objective. The present implementation supplies deterministic candidate templates, routed task evaluation, forced-action corpus checks, and evidence-bound policy admission.

2.2 Control-plane separation

OpenFlow exposes switch flow tables through an interface for adding and removing entries [1]. The corresponding NCP objects are activation predicates, W-ISA action programs, priorities, and rule lifetimes. The analogy concerns programmatic control and policy management; NCP’s matching signals are neural activations, and its actions modify selected parameter tensors within an inference scope.

2.3 Feedback-driven improvement

Self-Refine iteratively revises outputs using model-generated feedback [2]. Reflexion maintains linguistic feedback in episodic memory to influence later trials [3]. NCP instead makes a table of executable intervention rules the persistent optimization state. Its current synthesis step is a deterministic Python procedure driven by observed task labels and captured activations.

OPRO generates and evaluates candidate solutions using a language model conditioned on earlier solutions and their scores [12]. DSPy separates declarative language-model programs from metric-driven pipeline optimization [13]. These studies, also referenced by Takehi et al., provide context for separating candidate representation, proposal generation, and evaluation. NCP applies this separation to a table of activation-conditioned weight interventions.

2.4 Neural interventions

ROME and MEMIT construct parameter updates for factual associations [4, 5]. Contrastive Activation Addition derives behavioral directions from activation differences [6]. pyvene provides configurable intervention schemes [7], while NNsight supports tracing, persistent intervention definitions, and conditional execution [8]. These works provide related edit constructions and intervention infrastructures.

NCP builds on the W-ISA execution interface described in the companion manuscript [9]. W-ISA handles instruction validation, weight writes, snapshots, synchronization, and restoration. NCP handles the question of which program to propose, which evidence to collect, and which rule to admit.

2.5 Repetition and directional interventions

Pipis et al. [14] analyze looping in reasoning models, including its relationship to decoding temperature and temporally correlated errors. Their study motivates measuring repetition separately from answer correctness. NCP records token n-gram repetition, decoding-score entropy, and exact-answer outcomes as distinct signals. Arditi et al. [15] provide a related example of studying model behavior through a residual-stream direction; NCP’s current projection candidates use development-derived directions in a selected MLP input space.

3 System Model

Let fθf_{\theta} denote a pretrained model with registered base parameter state θ\theta. Let Φt\Phi_{t} be the active rule table at controller cycle tt, and AtA_{t} the archive of evaluated candidates. A request is routed through Φt\Phi_{t} to choose a program PP or the identity program.

The system’s persistent optimization state is

𝒮t=(Φt,At,et),\mathcal{S}_{t}=(\Phi_{t},A_{t},e_{t}),

where ete_{t} is the active-table version. The base parameter state remains the reference state between requests.

The control recurrence is

𝒯t=Observe⁡(fθ,Φt,Ddev),\mathcal{T}_{t}=\operatorname{Observe}(f_{\theta},\Phi_{t},D_{\mathrm{dev}}),
𝒞t=Synthesize⁡(𝒯t),\mathcal{C}_{t}=\operatorname{Synthesize}(\mathcal{T}_{t}),
(Φt+1,At+1)=Admit⁡(Φt,At,𝒞t,Dval,Cgate).(\Phi_{t+1},A_{t+1})=\operatorname{Admit}\bigl(\Phi_{t},A_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t},D_{\mathrm{val}},C_{\mathrm{gate}}\bigr).

Candidates are evaluated sequentially. Admission of an earlier candidate changes the policy context used to evaluate a later candidate. Repeated candidate identifiers retrieve their recorded decisions. A cycle with no new candidate evaluations terminates the current search.

This recurrence defines the control-policy layer of the RSI research program. Its objects are rule proposals, verification evidence, and active-policy transitions. The experiment in Section 7 records a cycle in which the archive grows and the active policy remains unchanged.

4 Neural Flow Table

4.1 Rule definition

A rule is represented as

r=(id,M,ℓ,v,τ,P,π,H,I,B),r=\bigl(\mathrm{id},\,M,\,\ell,\,v,\,\tau,\,P,\,\pi,\,H,\,I,\,B\bigr),

where MM identifies the base model; ℓ\ell specifies the activation module, input/output location, and pooling method; vv is a match direction; τ\tau is a threshold; PP is a W-ISA program; π\pi is priority; HH and II are hard and idle timeouts; and BB is an optional generation-token budget.

Model identity includes the model identifier, checkpoint revision, and a SHA-256 digest of parameter names, shapes, dtypes, and bytes. A rule fingerprint covers its definition and numeric operands. The table owns copies of submitted data.

For a nonzero captured activation hθℓ​(x)h_{\theta}^{\ell}(x) and nonzero direction vv, matching uses

sr​(x)=hθℓ​(x)T​v∥hθℓ​(x)∥2​∥v∥2,sr​(x)>τ.s_{r}(x)=\frac{h_{\theta}^{\ell}(x)^{T}v}{\lVert h_{\theta}^{\ell}(x)\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}},\hskip 20.00003pts_{r}(x)>\tau.

The implementation assigns score zero to a zero activation. Higher numeric priority is considered first, and equal-priority rules retain registration order. The first matching rule is selected. Activations are measured before the selected parameter intervention is applied.

4.2 Lifecycle and evidence

The table records candidate, active, rejected, expired, and retired states. Promotion requires accepted evidence for the rule’s fingerprint and the current active-table version. Changes to the active policy invalidate evidence measured against an earlier version.

Accepted rule definitions persist in the table. Their weight effects remain temporary and are reconstructed during matching requests. The runtime holds a shared model lock, applies the selected program, performs generation using a fresh KV cache, and restores the request-entry weights.

Hard timeout is elapsed wall-clock time since promotion. Idle timeout is elapsed time since promotion or the most recent completed selected request. Expiration is applied during table inspection for dispatch or admission; an in-flight request completes under its selected scope. Persisted timestamps preserve elapsed time across process restart. Token budgets are separate from these time-based fields.

Table snapshots preserve status, order, timestamps, hit counts, definitions, and evidence. Persistence writes a flushed temporary JSON file and atomically replaces the destination.

5 Telemetry and Candidate Synthesis

5.1 Output and task measurements

Each observation records generated text, token IDs, elapsed time, token-budget completion, and per-step entropy of the decoding-score distribution:

Ht=−∑jpt,jlogpt,j.H_{t}=-\sum_{j}p_{t,j}\log p_{t,j}.

Repetition telemetry uses token n-grams. For GG observed n-grams and UU distinct n-grams, the repeated fraction is

R=G−UG,R=\frac{G-U}{G},

with R=0R=0 when G=0G=0. The implementation also records the first adjacent repeated-block position and the maximum consecutive repetition run. The default n-gram size is four. Terminal EOS is removed from the repetition sequence.

Task scoring uses an explicit expected-answer specification. In the recorded fixture, the requested format ends with Final answer: <number>. The scorer takes the last answer-pattern capture, or the complete response when the pattern is absent, and applies case and trailing-period normalization before exact comparison.

5.2 Activation profiles

Development outcomes label prompt-end activations. When both classes are present, the profile is

verror=μfailure−μsuccess.v_{\mathrm{error}}=\mu_{\mathrm{failure}}-\mu_{\mathrm{success}}.

For an all-failure development set, the implementation uses verror=μfailurev_{\mathrm{error}}=\mu_{\mathrm{failure}} and records the source as failure_centroid. Capture and matching use the same activation site and pooling method. Zero-norm directions produce an empty candidate set for that site.

5.3 Deterministic action templates

For each configured transformer block and attention head, the initial synthesizer constructs:

The block and head dimensions are read from the loaded model. Candidate identifiers are deterministically derived from the action and matching configuration. Compilation checks the generated instruction sequence against the actual parameters before evaluation.

5.4 Controller-agnostic candidate representation

The NeuralRule representation separates a candidate’s origin from its execution and evaluation. It holds model identity, an activation predicate, a W-ISA source program, numeric operands and lifecycle fields. TorchBackend.compile() binds that source to the model through the W-ISA compiler. Caller-constructed rules can therefore use the supported instruction set independently of the templates in Section 5.3.

The public path is FlowTable.submit(rule), followed by Verifier.evaluate(rule,table,cases,corpus_tokens), and then promotion or rejection using the returned evidence. The verifier evaluates the proposed policy and the forced action; promotion checks the accepted flag, fingerprint and active-table version. These interfaces operate on trusted local rule and evidence data. The controller’s step() method assembles this path around the deterministic synthesizer used in the recorded experiment.

6 Verification and Policy Admission

6.1 Routed task comparison

The verifier evaluates the existing active table and the prospective table containing the candidate. Both runs use the same validation cases and the table’s actual priority order.

Let cc be the number of incorrect-to-correct transitions, rr the number of correct-to-incorrect transitions, mm the number of validation cases that selected the candidate, and

Δ​R=R¯before−R¯after.\Delta R=\bar{R}_{\mathrm{before}}-\bar{R}_{\mathrm{after}}.

The initial policy requires c≥1c\geq 1, r=0r=0, m>0m>0, and Δ​R≥0\Delta R\geq 0. Thresholds are caller-configurable. The gate also requires progress in task correctness or repetition: c>rc>r or Δ​R>0\Delta R>0.

6.2 Forced-action corpus comparison

The candidate program is forced active across the entire verifier corpus slice, independently of the trigger. This measurement evaluates the action under a common exposure protocol, while routed task evaluation measures the policy that would be deployed.

For mean token NLL ℓ¯0\bar{\ell}_{0} under original weights and ℓ¯P\bar{\ell}_{P} under the forced action, the relative perplexity change is

ΔPPL%=100[exp(ℓ¯P−ℓ¯0)−1].\Delta\mathrm{PPL}_{\%}=100\left[\exp(\bar{\ell}_{P}-\bar{\ell}_{0})-1\right].

The recorded policy sets a maximum increase of 0.5%. Original-corpus scores are cached by token digest and scoring protocol.

6.3 Spectral and restoration checks

For each edited parameter, the verifier records ∥W∥2\lVert W\rVert_{2}, ∥Δ​W∥2\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{2}, ∥Δ​W∥F\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{F}, and the relative spectral change. A configured relative spectral budget adds a corresponding admission condition.

Model parameter digests are checked around verification. The original weights are restored after each routed request and forced-action trial. Before promotion, evidence is checked against the candidate fingerprint and active-table version.

Under the recorded defaults, admission can be written as

Accept⁡(P)=\displaystyle\operatorname{Accept}(P)={} [m>0]∧[c≥1]∧[r=0]\displaystyle[m>0]\land[c\geq 1]\land[r=0]
∧[ΔR≥0]∧[ΔPPL%≤0.5]∧E,\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\land[\Delta R\geq 0]\land[\Delta\mathrm{PPL}_{\%}\leq 0.5]\land E,

where EE denotes exact parameter restoration and valid admission provenance. Configured spectral bounds are conjoined with this expression. Accepted candidates become active rules; other evaluated candidates retain their measurements and decision reasons in the archive.

7 Architectural Microbenchmark

7.1 Protocol

The recorded run uses HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM-135M-Instruct, revision b5f4b394abe60fe0e4d666139e57bfce520302a9, with FP32 weights on MPS and CPU FP64 intervention arithmetic. The runtime is PyTorch 2.15.0 with Python 3.12.9. Generation is greedy with a 128-token budget.

The nine-question handwritten fixture is an architectural microbenchmark of telemetry, candidate generation, admission and persistence. It contains three development, three validation, and three final-test questions with disjoint IDs and prompts. Development questions cover addition, sequence continuation, and counting grouped objects. Validation and final-test questions use separate arithmetic scenarios. Final-test inference begins after candidate selection finishes.

The language-modeling corpus is the cached WikiText-2 raw test split [10]. Its tokenized stream is partitioned into two disjoint 4,096-token slices. The first supplies the verifier corpus and the second supplies final corpus evaluation. Each slice scores 4,095 targets once, with context length 512 and stride 256. These are explicitly bounded corpus slices.

7.2 Generated candidates

Development exact-answer scoring was 0/3. Synthesis therefore used the failure centroid at the last prompt token’s input to model.layers.9.mlp.down_proj. This direction has 1,536 dimensions and norm 3.6363433948.

The three candidates target the tenth transformer block: an MLP projection, scaling query head 0’s output contribution by zero, and their ordered combination. The cosine threshold is 0.8. Each candidate was selected on all three validation prompts.

7.3 Task and corpus results

Baseline validation repetition fraction was 0.41333333. Baseline verifier perplexity was 23.74291741.

All three candidates met the configured perplexity budget. The corrected-answer threshold was one; the active table consequently remained at zero rules. The projection and head-scaling candidates reduced repetition, while their combination increased it under this fixture.

The MLP projection had relative spectral change 0.17329298; head scaling had 0.46918526. The combined program recorded both parameter changes separately. Every trial restored the base parameter digest.

Final exact-answer scoring was 0/3 for both original and routed execution. Both recorded a repetition fraction of 0.256. Final-slice baseline perplexity was 33.72129164. With the active policy unchanged, the final outputs matched the baseline policy.

7.4 Repeat, resume, and test coverage

The initial end-to-end run took 44.38 seconds. A new-process two-cycle run took 48.37 seconds and reproduced first-cycle generated outputs, token entropies, candidate fingerprints, spectral measurements, and perplexity values. Its second cycle recognized the three recorded candidate identifiers. A saved-table resume in a third process took 15.56 seconds and preserved the decisions and final outputs.

Independent reconstruction from the saved per-window NLL sums confirmed all 4,095 target counts and aggregate perplexity values. Direct reconstruction of corrected-case counts agreed with the admission records.

The NCP suite contains 25 passing tests. Controlled fixtures exercise both promotion and rejection through actual W-ISA parameter writes. Other cases cover hard and idle expiration, elapsed TTL across restart, stale evidence, priority shadowing, definition copying, token-budget dispatch, forced-action PPL for unmatched inputs, cancellation, and scalar-parameter fingerprints.

The recorded SmolLM run demonstrates the complete candidate-to-decision workflow and archive persistence. Its active-policy transition is Φt+1=Φt=∅\Phi_{t+1}=\Phi_{t}=\varnothing, with three evaluated candidates added to the archive. The controlled promotion fixtures exercise the complementary active-table transition.

8 Control-Policy Optimization

The optimization state has two parts with distinct effects. The active table changes inference routing, while the archive records search history. In the measured cycle the archive grew by three candidates and the active table stayed empty. On the next cycle, deterministic candidate identifiers retrieved the existing decisions. Saved-table resumption retained the same search state across process boundaries.

The verifier separates task progress from repetition and corpus cost. In the projection trial, repetition decreased by 0.19427160 and the forced-action corpus score satisfied the configured budget. The corrected-answer count remained zero, so the rule was archived under the one-correction admission criterion. This decision illustrates how the configured objective determines a policy transition rather than treating every change in an auxiliary signal as an improvement.

Proposal construction and acceptance remain separate operations. The representation in Section 5.4 carries a program regardless of its producer, while the verifier binds evidence to the exact candidate and current policy. Once a rule is active, priority matching and expiry determine its execution lifetime; the W-ISA scope determines the lifetime of its parameter effects.

The companion W-ISA study [9] measures this execution layer on SmolLM-135M and Qwen2.5-1.5B, including a 45-request comparison between materialized rank-one updates and equivalent PyTorch hooks. NCP’s microbenchmark measures the controller lifecycle on SmolLM. The shared abstraction is an explicit intervention program whose temporary weight effects are restored before the next policy evaluation.

9 Reproducibility and Implementation

The implementation contains the schema, flow table, telemetry, local backend, candidate synthesizer, verifier, and controller. It reuses W-ISA’s instruction compiler and request-scoped runtime. Public APIs include NeuralControlPlane, NeuralRule, FlowTable, TorchBackend, TaskCase, GatePolicy, and Verifier.

Rule tables are trusted local control data. Model identity, rule fingerprints, active-table versions, corpus-token hashes, and task fixtures are retained in the reports. Persistence uses a flushed temporary file followed by atomic replacement. Runtime scopes own parameter restoration; table promotion persists policy definitions.

Separate records retain the initial run, fresh-process repeat and saved-table resumption. The reasoning fixture defines expected answers and disjoint task splits; the tests exercise scoring and lifecycle transitions. The companion W-ISA manuscript [9] describes the execution substrate separately.

The experiment runner exposes options for the device, task fixture, corpus, candidate layers and heads, thresholds, timeouts, token budgets, and output location. Section 7 specifies the settings used for the recorded microbenchmark.

Code uses the MIT License, copyright 2026 Ekrem Aksoy. Model and corpus materials retain their upstream attribution and license terms.

10 Conclusion

NCP makes a language model’s intervention policy an explicit optimization state. Telemetry generates candidates; W-ISA executes them within owned scopes; a verifier evaluates routed task effects and forced-action corpus effects; and a versioned flow table records admission decisions. The initial local experiment produced three reproducible candidate evaluations, retained the configured correctness criterion, and restored the base model after every trial. This architecture provides a concrete basis for studying recursive self-improvement through successive, evidence-bound changes to neural flow policies.
